questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What makes a written policy real
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes a written policy operative rather than decorative
questions.stem: The clinic's information governance policy states that patient records may only be viewed for a care purpose. Which feature makes that policy real rather than decorative?

options.text: It is enforced by system rules and evidenced in audit trails, so departures are visible and countable
It is signed by the clinical director, so its authority is beyond question from that moment
options.misconception: believes a signature is what enforces a policy

options.text: It is filed in the governance folder, so every member of staff can be shown where it is kept
options.misconception: believes storage and visibility make a policy effective

options.text: It is reviewed annually, so the words inside it are always matched to current practice
options.misconception: believes periodic review keeps staff compliant

questions.explanation: A policy becomes real when it changes what people can do and the organisation can see whether it was followed. Audit trails and enforced rules supply that evidence, while a signature only proves the document exists.
questions.hint: Ask what stops and records a departure.

questions.stem: A ward note records that the clinic adopted an external accreditation standard, whose manual specifies required controls but no implementation detail. What does the standard itself settle?

options.text: The exact configuration of the clinic's systems, because the manual is written for implementation teams
options.misconception: believes a standard prescribes configuration detail

options.text: What must be achieved and evidenced, while leaving the method to the clinic to choose
The order of work for the project, because the manual sequences every implementation step
options.misconception: believes a standard sequences the work

options.text: The evidence that will be collected, since the manual names the exact documents for each control
options.misconception: believes a standard names the evidence documents

questions.explanation: A standard states the outcomes and the evidence expected of them, not the method. The method remains the clinic's choice, which is why two clinics can meet the same standard with different systems and still both be compliant.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: When a compensating control is acceptable
questions.learningObjective: Set out what makes a compensating control acceptable in place of the real one
questions.stem: The registrar notes that the clinic cannot yet enforce two-factor sign-in for the prescribing system. Explain what a compensating control must achieve for it to be acceptable.

answer.exemplar: A compensating control stands in for a control the clinic cannot apply, so it has to reduce the same risk rather than a different one, and the evidence has to show that it reduces it. If two-factor sign-in is unavailable, then the objective is to stop a stolen password being sufficient, and a compensating measure that addresses that directly, such as verified passcode entry before a controlled medication order is released, or session lock on a shared workstation with an audit trail of the operator, is credible. Several things would make it unacceptable. A control that merely adds a log without reducing the opportunity does not compensate, because the risk is unchanged. A control that is harder to bypass than the original is pointless. A control applied only to the clinicians who complained about it does not cover the population the standard was written for. And a compensating control without a named owner, a review date and a written rationale is an undocumented risk acceptance rather than a treatment, because the next reviewer will have no way to tell whether the reasoning still holds.

questions.explanation: A compensating control must address the same risk and demonstrably reduce it, not merely add paperwork. Without a named owner, a rationale and a review date it is an undocumented acceptance rather than a treatment.
questions.hint: Ask whether it reduces the same risk.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The fields a register entry needs
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a usable risk register entry must contain

stimulus.body: The risk register entry for the ward's shared workstation reads: risk 27, staff may leave a session open and expose patient records. The entry names no owner and no review date, lists no treatment beyond a laminated sign on the wall, and records the residual risk as low. The governance lead noted that the risk was raised two years ago and has not been revisited since the ward moved to a new building.

questions.stem: According to the clinic register above, what should the governance lead record?

options.text: The residual rating is wrong, because a laminated sign cannot lower a risk at all
options.misconception: focuses on the rating rather than the missing fields

options.text: The entry needs a documented rationale, because the rating was accepted without explanation
options.misconception: targets the rationale while ignoring ownership

options.text: The entry is incomplete, since it lacks an owner, a review date and any real treatment
The entry should be closed, because the ward has moved and the old workstation risk is gone
options.misconception: assumes a move removes the underlying exposure

questions.explanation: A register entry has to say who owns the risk, when it is next reviewed, how it is being treated and what risk remains. This entry has none of those, so it cannot be managed, and a sign on a wall is not a treatment for an unattended session.
questions.hint: Ask what a register entry must name.

options.misconception: assumes ownership carries unlimited budget and duty

options.text: To record the risk, and to accept every residual level the board sets without comment

options.misconception: assumes ownership guarantees absence of harm

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a standard specifies and what it does not
questions.learningObjective: Explain the local decisions an adopted standard leaves open
questions.stem: The clinic's board adopts an accreditation standard and the clinical lead asks what it must still decide locally. Explain what the standard leaves to the organisation.

answer.exemplar: The standard settles the outcome and the evidence, so the board is not free to choose a weaker result. What it still decides is the method. For each requirement the clinic has to select or build a control that produces the required evidence in a way that fits its own clinical workflow, and it has to be able to defend that choice to an auditor. That means answering practical questions the standard never answers: which system holds the record, who performs the check, how often it runs, what happens when it fails, and who reviews the results. A useful discipline is to write the objective in the clinic's own words first and only then map it to the standard's wording, because a requirement mapped first tends to produce a control that satisfies the text without satisfying the intent. The standard also leaves the scope of applicability, the treatment of exceptional cases such as emergency access, and the retention of evidence to the organisation.

questions.explanation: The standard fixes the required outcome and evidence but not the method, scope or exception handling. Those choices stay with the clinic and have to be defensible to an auditor.
questions.hint: Ask which decisions the wording leaves open.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A control objective and the thing that implements it
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether an implemented control satisfies its control objective

stimulus.body: The ward audit recorded one control objective as: only registered clinicians who are part of the patient's care team may open the discharge summary. The objective was then mapped to a rule that permits access when the clinician appears on the patient's episode record, and the audit tested 40 discharges by opening each summary with two clinician accounts. In 38 cases the rule behaved as intended; in 2 cases the account of a locum who had covered the ward opened a summary for a patient they had not been involved in.

questions.stem: According to the audit note above, which reading is correct?

options.text: The objective is met, because 38 of 40 tests behaved as the rule intended
options.misconception: treats a high pass rate as a met objective

options.text: The rule failed, because it permits access for any clinician who appears anywhere on the episode record
options.misconception: criticises the rule without comparing it to the objective

options.text: The objective is only partly met, since the implemented control permits access beyond care team membership
The objective is not met at all, because 2 failures mean the control does not work
options.misconception: treats partial failure as total failure

questions.explanation: The objective is about care team membership, and the implemented rule is broader, so the two failures show a gap between the control and the objective it is meant to satisfy. The audit should record the objective as partly met and describe the specific gap, rather than reporting a percentage.
questions.hint: Ask whether the control matches the objective.

questions.topic: When a compensating control is acceptable
questions.learningObjective: State the test for a compensating control and what defeats it

options.misconception: confines the compensating control to one control type

options.text: It must be cheaper than the recommended control, and it would be ruled out if it cost more to run
options.misconception: makes cost the test of a compensating control

options.text: It must cover the same printer, and it would be ruled out if it protected a different device

options.text: It must reduce the same risk, and it would be ruled out if it merely recorded events

questions.learningObjective: Interpret what naming a risk owner commits them to
questions.stem: The clinic's medication error log names a pharmacy technician as the owner of the residual dispensing risk. What does that ownership mean in practice?

options.misconception: mistakes ownership for a guarantee of safety

options.text: The technician is accountable for reducing that risk and escalating what exceeds their authority
The technician funds any control needed to bring the risk below the clinic's tolerance

options.text: The technician is accountable only for recording the risk and the actions taken against it
options.misconception: reduces ownership to note taking

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Matching a treatment to the kind of risk
questions.learningObjective: Explain how two different risks need different treatments
questions.stem: The clinic faces two risks on the ward: staff sharing a login and a supplier being unable to provide support overnight. Explain how the right treatments differ.

answer.exemplar: The two risks have different causes, so the same treatment will not work on both. A shared login is a practice risk that arises inside the clinic and is reduced by changing practice: individual accounts, no shared passwords, and a short session timeout on shared workstations. It is not transferred, because a supplier cannot take responsibility for how the clinic's staff behave, and avoiding it would mean stopping clinical staff from using the system at all, which would be disproportionate. A supplier that cannot provide overnight support is a dependency risk whose consequence is financial and contractual, so it is better treated by transferring part of it, for example through a contractual support commitment with a defined response time, or by insuring against the outage cost. Either way, the treatment has to fit the mechanism of the risk rather than the level of the score, because a low-scoring risk with the wrong treatment stays where it is.

questions.explanation: A practice risk is reduced by changing practice, while a dependency risk is often transferred contractually or financially. The treatment has to match the mechanism of the risk rather than its score.
questions.hint: Ask what causes each risk.

questions.topic: What makes a written policy real
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a policy review that separates missing evidence from broken practice

stimulus.body: The clinic's information governance group reviewed its 26 information policies. For 19 of them the group held audit evidence showing the rule had been applied during the year. For 4 policies the group held only the signed document and no operational evidence, and for 3 policies the review noted that staff were doing something the policy said they must not. The group noted that two of the policies without evidence had been in place for more than five years.

questions.stem: According to the governance note above, which conclusion is sound?

options.text: Nineteen of the policies are working, and the remaining seven are outside the scope of the review
options.misconception: treats missing evidence as scope exclusion

options.text: All 26 policies need rewriting, because policies without evidence have no effect on staff at all
options.misconception: prescribes rewriting where evidence gathering is needed

options.text: Seven policies lack evidence of operation and three show practice contrary to the rule
The clinic cannot rely on any of the policies, because evidence was missing for a quarter of them
options.misconception: generalises a minority gap to the whole set

questions.explanation: The review separates policies with evidence of operation from those without, and it identifies three where practice contradicts the rule. Those need a different response from the four that simply lack evidence, so treating them as one group hides the difference.
questions.hint: Ask what is missing versus what is being broken.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a risk owner actually carries
questions.learningObjective: Explain the scope of accountability carried by a risk owner
questions.stem: The clinical lead asks what the ward pharmacist carries when a risk is assigned to their role. Explain the scope of that accountability.

answer.exemplar: Owning a risk means the owner is accountable for it in the sense that they must be able to show what is being done about it, that what is being done is proportionate, and that anything they cannot influence has been escalated rather than quietly tolerated. In practice for a pharmacist that means agreeing the control, making sure it operates, checking the evidence that it operated, and reporting when the residual risk sits above the level the clinic says it will accept. It also means the owner is expected to say so when a risk is misassigned. A risk parked with a role that cannot act on it produces a register entry that looks covered while nothing changes, and the assignment itself then becomes the failure. Ownership does not mean the owner personally guarantees that no harm occurs, it does not mean the owner funds whatever control might be needed, and it does not mean the owner may accept a residual level that the clinic has said is above tolerance without recording that acceptance explicitly.

questions.explanation: Ownership means being accountable for acting on the risk within the authority held and escalating the rest. It is not a personal guarantee, a funding obligation, or permission to accept an out-of-tolerance residual silently.
questions.hint: Ask what the owner must be able to show.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: When a compensating control is acceptable
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a compensating control should be justified for a temporary arrangement
questions.stem: The clinic must keep a temporary local server for an old radiology system for six months. Explain how a compensating control should be justified for that period.

answer.exemplar: The justification has to show that the temporary arrangement reduces the same risk as the control it stands in for, for the same reason and no weaker. If the recommended control would have been network segregation between the old system and the clinical network, then the compensating arrangement must keep the old system out of the clinical network by some other means, such as a dedicated segment with no route to clinical workstations, and it must be evidenced in a way that shows the isolation held rather than assumed. A compensating control that merely limits who may log on, without fixing the network exposure, does not address the risk the segregation was chosen for. The period needs its own controls: an expiry date, a named owner responsible for removing the arrangement, and evidence collected during the period that the isolation is still intact, because a temporary measure that is never checked becomes a permanent one by default. The reason for the delay should also be written down, since a reader will ask whether the arrangement is still necessary, and the answer has to be an evidenced position rather than a habit.

questions.explanation: A compensating control must reduce the same risk for the same reason, be evidenced, and carry an expiry date with a named owner. A temporary arrangement without those becomes permanent by default.
questions.hint: Ask whether the same risk is reduced and when it ends.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a standard specifies and what it does not
questions.learningObjective: Set out the right order for adopting a clinical information standard
questions.stem: The registrar asks how the clinic should go about adopting a national clinical information standard. Explain the sequence and why the order matters.

answer.exemplar: The order matters because a standard read from the beginning produces controls that satisfy the wording rather than the intent. The clinic should start with its own objectives, written in the words the clinical team actually use: a nurse should be able to read the objective and tell whether the ward is doing it. The team then reads the standard and maps each objective to the clause that covers it, checking as they go whether a clause is satisfied by the objective or merely resembles it. Where a clause has no objective behind it, the team has found either a gap in its practice or a requirement it genuinely does not apply, and that has to be recorded either way. Only then does the team select controls, and at that point the standard's evidence requirement shapes what the control must leave behind, so selecting controls before reading the evidence requirement usually means building something and then discovering it produces the wrong artefact. The last step is a dry run against real records, because the standard's expectations rarely match the shape of the data the clinic actually has.

questions.explanation: Write the objectives first, then map them to clauses, then choose controls against the evidence requirement, then test on real records. Doing it the other way round builds controls that satisfy the wording rather than the intent.
questions.hint: Ask what the controls will have to produce.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Matching a treatment to the kind of risk
questions.learningObjective: Explain why access and dependency risks take different treatments
questions.stem: The clinic faces a risk of a patient record being viewed by a colleague not involved in that patient's care, and a risk of a supplier withdrawing support. Explain why the treatments differ.

answer.exemplar: The two risks differ in their mechanism rather than in their score, and that is what the treatment has to follow. The record viewing risk exists because staff can reach records they have no need for, so it is reduced by changing access, for example by tying the ability to open a summary to the care team on the episode and by reviewing who holds broad search rights. Nothing is gained by trying to transfer it, because a colleague's access is the clinic's own to manage, and avoiding it would mean stopping colleagues from seeing records at all. The supplier withdrawal risk is a dependency whose consequence is operational and financial, so it is better handled by transfer or by reducing the dependency: a contractual support commitment, or consolidating onto a platform the clinic could support itself. The useful test is to ask what mechanism produces the risk. If the mechanism is something the clinic does, the treatment changes that practice, and if the mechanism is a counterparty's decision, the treatment changes the contract or removes the dependency.

questions.explanation: A risk caused by the clinic's own access practice is reduced by changing that practice, while a dependency risk is transferred contractually or reduced by removing the dependency. The mechanism, not the score, picks the treatment.
questions.hint: Ask what mechanism produces each risk.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a risk owner actually carries
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a risk assignment obliges and what it does not fix
questions.stem: The clinic assigns the risk of delayed imaging results to the radiology lead. Explain what that assignment obliges and what the assignment does not fix.

answer.exemplar: The assignment obliges the lead to be answerable for the risk in a specific and limited sense: they must be able to show what is being done to reduce it, that the measures are proportionate, and that any part they cannot influence has been escalated to someone who can. They must also keep the register entry current and bring it back for review at the agreed date. What the assignment does not do is settle the risk's causes or its consequences. Naming the lead does not make staffing, reporting schedules or equipment availability any different, and it does not create the authority to change any of those things. It is also not a guarantee: an owned risk can still occur, and the ownership exists so that when it does there is a named person who has to answer for what was and was not done about it. The failure mode this arrangement is designed to prevent is the register entry that nobody holds, where the risk sits in a spreadsheet with no owner and therefore no pressure on anyone until an incident forces the issue.

questions.explanation: The assignment makes the lead accountable for acting on the risk and escalating what they cannot change. It does not change the causes or the consequences, and it is not a guarantee that the risk will not occur.
questions.hint: Ask what the owner can actually change.

questions.topic: When a compensating control is acceptable
questions.learningObjective: Design and evidence a compensating control for a legacy arrangement
questions.stem: The clinic must operate its legacy bedside system for a further year. Explain how the compensating control for that arrangement should be designed and evidenced.

answer.exemplar: The compensating control has to address the same risk as the control it stands in for, and it has to be evidenced on its own terms rather than by pointing at the standard. If the recommended control was that the legacy system never holds identifiable patient data, then the compensating arrangement must actually achieve that, for example by holding only an episode reference on the bedside device with the identifiers resolved at the point of use through the main record, and it must be evidenced by a periodic check that the legacy store contains no identifiers rather than by a policy statement saying it should not. Three design points matter. The arrangement should be as narrow as the risk allows, because every extra exception adds exposure that has to be argued for separately. It should have an expiry date and a named owner, because a legacy arrangement without an end date becomes permanent through drift rather than through decision. And it should be reviewed on a schedule with evidence collected each time, so that the question is never whether the compensation still works but when it was last demonstrated to work.

questions.explanation: The compensating arrangement must reduce the same risk, be evidenced by its own checks, stay as narrow as possible, and carry an expiry date with a named owner and a fixed review.
questions.hint: Ask how the risk will be shown to be reduced.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The fields a register entry needs
questions.learningObjective: Identify a register entry whose treatment has stopped operating

stimulus.body: The community clinic's register entry 3 covers the risk that a patient is given a repeat prescription without a recent review. The entry describes the risk, names the prescriber as the owner, records the treatment as a system block on repeat requests older than 12 months, records the residual rating as medium, and carries a review date of 31 January. The note adds that the block was switched off in November to clear a backlog and had not been switched back on.

questions.stem: From the clinic note above, what is the finding?

options.text: The entry is complete and the treatment is working, because the register records all four required fields
options.misconception: confuses a complete entry with an operating treatment

options.text: The residual rating is wrong, because a system block would have reduced the risk to low
options.misconception: assumes a rating without evidence

options.text: The treatment has stopped operating, so the recorded residual rating no longer holds
The entry should be removed, because the risk was treated and the register should reflect that
options.misconception: assumes a suspended control removes the risk

questions.explanation: The entry is complete, but the control behind the recorded rating was switched off and never restored, so the treatment is not operating and the medium rating is unevidenced.
questions.hint: Ask whether the recorded control is still running.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a risk owner actually carries
questions.learningObjective: Separate risk ownership from owning a related process
questions.stem: The clinic's consent record risk is owned by the complaints manager. First state what the ownership obliges, then state what it does not oblige.

options.text: To respond to every complaint within five working days, and to apologise where harm occurred
options.misconception: confuses ownership with a specific response duty

options.text: To ensure consent forms are used in every clinic, and to audit their completion each month
options.misconception: assumes ownership extends to operating the control

options.text: To maintain the complaints log, and to report its numbers to the board each quarter
options.misconception: reduces ownership to record keeping and reporting

options.text: To reduce the risk within their authority and to escalate what they cannot change

questions.explanation: Ownership is accountability for acting on the risk within the role's authority and escalating what exceeds it. It is not ownership of the complaints process, the consent process or the reporting cycle, even where the owner works on them.
questions.hint: Ask what the owner must escalate.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Accepting a residual risk as a decision
questions.learningObjective: Frame an above-tolerance residual risk acceptance correctly
questions.stem: The governance group is asked to accept a residual risk of 4 where the clinic's tolerance for that risk is 2. Which framing of that acceptance is correct?

options.text: A recorded, time-limited decision with an owner, an expiry and a review date
A permanent decision, since revisiting the residual risk would undermine confidence in the clinic
options.misconception: treats acceptance as permanent rather than reviewed

options.text: A note that the risk has been considered, which is enough while the treatment remains in place
options.misconception: mistakes a note for a governance decision

options.text: An assurance from the clinical team that the residual level is acceptable to them
options.misconception: accepts an assurance in place of a decision

questions.explanation: Accepting a risk above tolerance needs an owner, a rationale and an expiry, so it is reviewed rather than inherited. A note that it was considered is weaker than the decision required.
questions.hint: Ask what makes the acceptance reviewable.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Matching a treatment to the kind of risk
questions.learningObjective: Read a set of matched risk and treatment pairings
questions.stem: The clinic's register records two treatments against two risks. A risk of a patient receiving the wrong dose is paired with a double-check at the pharmacy, and a risk of a supplier ending support is paired with a contractual support commitment. What does the pairing show?

options.text: The clinic applies the same treatment style to both risks, which keeps the register consistent
options.misconception: reads consistency as the aim rather than fit

options.text: Each treatment matches how its risk arises, since one is a practice change and one is a transfer
The supplier risk is underestimated, because a contractual commitment never reduces a risk
options.misconception: believes contractual terms never reduce a risk

options.text: The pharmacy risk should also be transferred, because transfer is the stronger treatment
options.misconception: assumes transfer is always the stronger treatment

questions.explanation: A double-check at the pharmacy reduces a risk caused by the clinic's own steps, while a contractual commitment shifts part of a supplier dependency risk to the counterparty. Each treatment fits the mechanism of its risk.
questions.hint: Ask how each of the two risks arises.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What makes a written policy real
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the policies that are both evidenced and not contradicted
questions.stem: The clinic's governance review covered 30 policies and found 22 with audit evidence of operation in the year. Eight policies had no operational evidence, and 4 of those 8 were found to be contradicted by practice. How many policies are both evidenced as operating and not contradicted in practice?
questions.explanation: The 22 policies with evidence of operation are the ones not contradicted, since the 4 contradicted policies come from the group with no evidence. So 22 policies are both evidenced as operating and not contradicted in practice.
questions.hint: The contradicted policies sit outside the evidenced group.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a standard specifies and what it does not
questions.learningObjective: Explain what an adopted national standard will and will not decide
questions.stem: The clinical governance lead asks what the new national standard will and will not tell the clinic to do. Explain the distinction.

answer.exemplar: The standard will tell the clinic what it must achieve and what evidence will demonstrate it, which is the part that cannot be traded away and the part an auditor will test. It will not tell the clinic how to achieve it. The implementation may sit in the electronic record system, in a paper checklist completed at the bedside or in a ward routine that a manager checks, and all three can satisfy the same requirement. The standard will also not decide which parts of the clinic the requirement applies to, because a small unit, a teaching hospital and an outpatient clinic will have different scopes, and it will not decide how exceptional cases such as emergency access are handled. The practical consequence is that adopting a standard is a design exercise rather than a procurement one, and the clinic needs people who can write the objective in clinical language, map it to the clause, choose a control that will actually produce the required artefact and then test that choice against real records before claiming compliance.

questions.explanation: The standard fixes the outcome and the evidence but leaves the method, the scope and the exception handling to the organisation. Adopting it is therefore a design exercise, not a procurement one.
questions.hint: Ask what the clause obliges the clinic to show.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A control objective and the thing that implements it
questions.learningObjective: Weigh a control that permits self-certification or bypass

stimulus.body: The medicines audit set an objective: a second check must be recorded before a high risk medicine is administered. The control chosen was an electronic prompt requiring the second checker's identifier before the administration record can be closed. Testing covered 60 administrations of high risk medicines, and in 57 cases a second identifier was present. In 2 cases the identifier had been entered by the person who gave the medicine, and in 1 case the administration record was closed on the paper fallback with no second check recorded at all.

questions.stem: From the audit note above, what does the clinic record?

options.text: The control is effective, because 57 of 60 administrations met the requirement
options.misconception: treats a high pass rate as full compliance

options.text: The control is ineffective, because the paper fallback allows the prompt to be bypassed
options.misconception: condemns the whole control over a single route

options.text: The objective is only partly met, since the control can be self-certified or bypassed
The control should be withdrawn, because the fallback makes verification impossible to enforce
options.misconception: proposes removing a control rather than tightening it

questions.explanation: The objective requires a second check by someone else, and the control allowed self-certification and closure with no check. The audit should record the objective as partly met and name those two routes.
questions.hint: Ask who performed the second check.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: When a compensating control is acceptable
questions.learningObjective: State the compensating control test and the governance conditions attached
questions.stem: The clinic cannot yet implement full encryption on the shared diagnostic workstations. First state what a compensating control must achieve, then state what the governance group should require alongside it.

options.text: It must cover the workstations, and the group should require an annual attestation by the ward manager
options.misconception: confines compensation to one device type and a weak review

options.text: It must be free, and the group should require a written statement that no data is sensitive
options.misconception: makes cost and assertion the test of adequacy

options.text: It must be enforced by the supplier, and the group should require a progress report each quarter
options.misconception: delegates the control and the review to a third party

options.text: It must reduce the same risk, and the group should require an owner, an expiry and evidence

questions.explanation: A compensating control must reduce the same risk the encryption was meant to address, and without an owner, an expiry and evidence that it operated it is an undocumented acceptance.
questions.hint: Ask whether the same risk is reduced and who owns it.
